lessons.title: Estrus Detection and Teasing Techniques
lessons.body:
Estrus detection is the foundation of any successful breeding program. In Africa, where many mares run on pasture or in group housing, you must observe them carefully twice daily, ideally at dawn and dusk when temperatures are cooler and horses are active. A mare in heat (estrus) will show specific signs when exposed to a stallion or a teaser. The most reliable sign is 'winking' â the opening and closing of the vulva â often accompanied by squatting, urinating frequently, and tail raising. She may also stand still for the stallion, whereas a mare not in heat will kick, squeal, and move away.

Use a teaser stallion that is calm and easy to handle. If you don't have a stallion, a vigorous gelding or even a pony can work, but stallions are more effective. Tease the mare over a sturdy fence or in a small pen. Keep sessions short â 5 to 10 minutes per mare â to avoid fatigue and injury. Record everything: date, time, intensity of signs (score 1 to 5), and any changes. Many African breeders use a simple notebook or a smartphone app to track cycles.

For mares that show weak or silent heats, try teasing them with a stallion across a barrier for 15 minutes daily. Some mares need to be teased in the presence of other mares to stimulate signs. If a mare still shows nothing after 21 days, she may be in anestrus (not cycling) due to poor nutrition, heavy parasite load, or the season. In tropical Africa, mares often cycle year-round, but in cooler highland areas, they may be seasonal (spring to autumn).

Practical tips: Wear gloves and boots when handling mares near a stallion. Avoid teasing during the hottest part of the day (11amâ3pm). Keep a calendar â the estrous cycle averages 21 days (range 18â24), with estrus lasting 5â7 days. If you breed on the first day of standing heat, you are often too early. The best time is 24â48 hours after she first stands for the teaser, or every other day during heat. Always confirm with a veterinarian using ultrasound if possible.

lessons.title: Ultrasound Examination of the Reproductive Tract
lessons.body:
Ultrasound is the most powerful tool for managing mare reproduction, but many African breeders lack access. If you can afford it, a portable ultrasound machine (linear probe, 5â7.5 MHz) costs from $3,000 to $8,000. Alternatively, you can hire a veterinarian who owns one. The exam is quick (5â10 minutes) and safe. You will need a chute or stocks to restrain the mare, plus a tail wrap and a clean sleeve.

The vet will insert a gloved, lubricated arm into the rectum and hold the ultrasound probe against the reproductive tract. On the screen, you will see the uterus and ovaries. Key things to identify: follicles (fluid-filled black circles) on the ovaries, the corpus luteum (a solid grey area after ovulation), and any fluid or abnormalities in the uterus. A follicle of 35 mm or larger usually means the mare will ovulate within 24â48 hours. This is the best time to breed or inseminate.

For pregnancy diagnosis, ultrasound can detect an embryonic vesicle as early as 14 days after ovulation. In Africa, where transport to a clinic may be difficult, learning to do basic ultrasound yourself can save money and time. Many agricultural colleges offer short courses. You can also use a technique called 'rectal palpation' without ultrasound â feeling the uterus and ovaries with your hand â but it is less accurate and requires experience.

Practical use: Scan mares every 2â3 days during heat to track follicle growth. If you are using artificial insemination (AI) with chilled or frozen semen, ultrasound helps you time insemination precisely. After breeding, scan at 14â16 days for pregnancy, then again at 28â30 days to confirm a heartbeat. If the mare is not pregnant, you can restart the cycle sooner. In areas with high tick-borne diseases, scan for uterine cysts or infections that can cause infertility. Always clean the probe and wear new gloves between mares to prevent disease spread.

lessons.title: Manipulation of the Estrous Cycle
lessons.body:
Manipulating the mare's cycle lets you breed at a convenient time, synchronize mares for a stallion, or treat problem breeders. The most common method in Africa is using hormones. Prostaglandin F2Î± (e.g., dinoprost or cloprostenol) is used to shorten the luteal phase. If a mare has a corpus luteum (days 5â14 after ovulation), a single injection of 5 mg dinoprost will bring her into heat in 2â4 days. This is useful if you missed a breeding or want to breed several mares at once.

For mares that are not cycling (anestrus), you can use a progesterone-releasing device (like a CIDR or PRID) inserted into the vagina for 7â14 days, often combined with estradiol. When removed, most mares come into heat within 2â5 days. In Africa, these devices may be expensive or unavailable, so some breeders use a simpler method: daily injections of progesterone in oil for 10â14 days, then stop. The mare will ovulate 5â7 days after the last injection.

Another technique is 'short cycling': give prostaglandin, then breed on the next heat. This works well for mares with normal cycles. For mares with prolonged heat or anovulatory follicles, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) â 1500â2500 IU â can be given when a follicle reaches 35 mm to induce ovulation within 36â48 hours. This is especially helpful with frozen semen, which requires precise timing.

Practical cautions: Hormones must be stored correctly (refrigerated, protected from light). Use sterile needles and syringes. Never use prostaglandin on a pregnant mare â it will cause abortion. If you are unsure of pregnancy status, scan first. In hot climates, work early morning to reduce stress. Record all treatments and observe for signs of heat daily. If a mare does not respond, check for nutritional deficiencies (especially energy and protein) or uterine infection. Always consult a veterinarian before starting a synchronization program, as incorrect use can cause cysts or persistent heat.

lessons.title: Breeding Soundness Examination of the Mare
lessons.body:
A breeding soundness examination (BSE) tells you if a mare is likely to conceive and carry a foal. It is essential before buying a mare or starting a breeding season. In Africa, where veterinary services may be limited, you can do a basic exam yourself, but a full BSE requires a vet with ultrasound and a speculum. The exam has four parts: history, physical exam, reproductive exam, and sometimes laboratory tests.

History: Ask about previous foals, heat cycles, any abortions, retained placenta, or difficult births. Note her age â mares over 15 years may have reduced fertility. Physical exam: check body condition score (BCS). A mare should be 5â7 on a 9-point scale. Thin mares (BCS <4) often don't cycle; obese mares (BCS >8) may have trouble conceiving. Look at the udder, vulva, and perineum. A 'sunken' vulva or poor perineal conformation can allow air and bacteria into the vagina, causing infection.

Reproductive exam: The vet will use a speculum to look at the cervix and vagina for discharge, tears, or tumors. Then, rectal palpation and ultrasound to assess the uterus (size, tone, fluid) and ovaries (follicles, cysts). A uterine culture and cytology can identify bacteria like Streptococcus zooepidemicus or fungi. In Africa, common problems include endometritis (uterine infection) from poor hygiene during breeding, and ovarian cysts. A biopsy may be taken to check for fibrosis (scarring) â a common cause of infertility in older mares.

Practical interpretation: A mare with a clean culture, normal uterus, and regular cycles is sound. If abnormalities are found, treatment may include uterine lavage with saline, antibiotics, or hormones. For mares with poor perineal conformation, a Caslick's suture (stitching the top of the vulva) can prevent contamination. Always do a BSE at least 30 days before breeding. If you are buying a mare, ask for a written report. In many African countries, a BSE costs $50â$150, which is small compared to the cost of feeding a barren mare for a year.

lessons.title: Managing the Problem Mare
lessons.body:
A 'problem mare' is one that fails to conceive after three breeding cycles, or has repeated early pregnancy loss. In Africa, common causes include poor nutrition, uterine infection, hormonal imbalances, and anatomical defects. Managing these mares requires patience and a systematic approach. First, review her history: when was she last bred? Did she conceive? Was there any discharge? Then, do a full breeding soundness exam.

Uterine infection (endometritis) is the most common problem. Signs include a cloudy or bloody discharge, short cycles, and failure to conceive. Treatment: uterine lavage with 1â2 liters of warm saline, followed by infusion of antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin or ceftiofur) for 3â5 days. In Africa, where antibiotics may be scarce, you can use a dilute povidone-iodine solution (0.2%) for lavage, but never use strong chemicals. Repeat the lavage daily until the fluid is clear. Also, ensure the mare is teased and bred with clean technique â use a sterile sleeve and lubricant for AI.

Hormonal problems: Some mares have persistent follicles that don't ovulate (anovulatory follicles). Give hCG (1500â2500 IU) when the follicle is >35 mm. If she has a corpus luteum that persists (prolonged diestrus), prostaglandin will bring her back into heat. For mares with low progesterone after breeding, supplement with altrenogest (Regumate) orally for 14 days. This is expensive but can save a pregnancy.

Anatomical defects: A 'sunken' anus or poor vulvar seal can cause pneumovagina (air in the vagina). A Caslick's suture is a simple surgical fix â the vet stitches the top of the vulva, leaving a small opening for urine. This prevents fecal contamination and air. For mares with cervical tears, surgery may be needed. In all cases, improve nutrition: feed a balanced diet with 12â14% protein, good quality forage, and minerals (especially copper and selenium). Provide shade and fresh water. If a mare still fails after 6 months of treatment, consider embryo transfer or retiring her as a broodmare. Always consult a veterinarian before using hormones or antibiotics.

lessons.title: Nutritional Management for Reproductive Health
lessons.body:
Nutrition is the single most important factor affecting a mare's ability to conceive and carry a foal. In Africa, where pastures vary from lush to dry, you must adjust feeding to her reproductive stage. A mare at maintenance (not pregnant, not lactating) needs about 1.5â2% of her body weight in dry matter per day. For a 500 kg mare, that is 7.5â10 kg of hay or pasture. If she is thin (body condition score <4), she will not cycle. Increase energy with grains like oats, maize, or barley â up to 0.5 kg per 100 kg body weight. But avoid overfeeding: obese mares (BCS >8) have more difficulty conceiving and foaling.

During early pregnancy (first 5 months), the foal grows slowly. Feed a maintenance diet plus a vitamin-mineral supplement. From month 6 onward, the foal grows rapidly. Increase energy by 10â20% and protein to 12â14%. Good sources of protein in Africa include lucerne (alfalfa) hay, cottonseed meal, and sunflower meal. Provide free-choice minerals, especially calcium, phosphorus, copper, zinc, and selenium. In many African soils, selenium is deficient, so use a supplement containing 1â2 mg selenium per day. Iodine is also important for foal thyroid development.

After foaling, a lactating mare needs 2â3 times more energy and protein than a dry mare. She may lose weight, so feed 2â3 kg of concentrate per day plus good hay. Always provide clean water â a lactating mare drinks 50â80 liters daily. In hot climates, add electrolytes to water if she sweats heavily. Monitor body condition weekly. If she drops below BCS 4, increase feed immediately. For mares that are hard keepers, add oil (e.g., 250 ml vegetable oil per day) for extra energy. Avoid sudden feed changes â introduce new feeds over 7â10 days. Also, ensure she has access to salt licks. Finally, keep her free of internal parasites (deworm every 8â12 weeks) and external parasites (ticks, flies) that can transmit diseases. A well-fed mare is your best guarantee for a healthy foal.

quiz.q: What is the most reliable sign that a mare is in estrus?
options: B) Winking of the vulva and squatting
D) Running away from other mares
quiz.explanation: Winking and squatting are classic signs of estrus when a mare is exposed to a stallion.

quiz.q: How often should you tease a mare for estrus detection?
options: D) Only when she shows signs
quiz.explanation: Twice daily teasing (morning and evening) helps catch the onset of heat accurately.

quiz.q: What is the average length of the estrous cycle in a mare?
quiz.explanation: The mare's estrous cycle averages 21 days, ranging from 18 to 24 days.

quiz.q: When is the best time to breed a mare during her heat?
options: A) On the first day of standing heat
B) 24â48 hours after she first stands for the teaser
C) On the last day of heat
quiz.explanation: Ovulation usually occurs 24â48 hours after the onset of standing heat, so breeding then maximizes conception.

quiz.q: What does a follicle of 35 mm or larger on ultrasound indicate?
options: B) The mare will ovulate within 24â48 hours
C) The mare has an infection
D) The mare is in anestrus
quiz.explanation: A follicle of 35 mm or more is pre-ovulatory and indicates imminent ovulation.

quiz.q: How early can ultrasound detect a pregnancy in a mare?
quiz.explanation: An embryonic vesicle can be seen on ultrasound as early as 14 days post-ovulation.

quiz.q: Which hormone is used to shorten the luteal phase and bring a mare into heat?
quiz.explanation: Prostaglandin F2Î± lyses the corpus luteum, causing the mare to return to estrus.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a CIDR or PRID in cycle manipulation?
options: B) To suppress estrus and then synchronize heat after removal
quiz.explanation: Progesterone-releasing devices suppress estrus; removal leads to a synchronized heat.

quiz.q: When should hCG be given to induce ovulation?
options: A) When the follicle is 20 mm
B) When the follicle is 35 mm or larger
quiz.explanation: hCG is effective when given with a follicle of at least 35 mm to induce ovulation within 36â48 hours.

quiz.q: Why should prostaglandin never be given to a pregnant mare?
options: C) It makes her infertile forever
quiz.explanation: Prostaglandin causes luteolysis, which will terminate a pregnancy by removing progesterone support.

quiz.q: What is a key part of a breeding soundness examination?
quiz.explanation: Uterine culture and cytology help identify infections that can cause infertility.

quiz.q: What body condition score (BCS) is ideal for a broodmare?
quiz.explanation: A BCS of 5â7 is associated with optimal reproductive performance.

quiz.q: What is a Caslick's suture used for?
options: A) To close a cervical tear
B) To prevent pneumovagina and fecal contamination
quiz.explanation: Caslick's suture stitches the upper vulva to prevent air and feces from entering the vagina.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common cause of infertility in older mares?
quiz.explanation: Ovarian cysts and uterine fibrosis are both common in older mares and reduce fertility.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating mare drink daily?
quiz.explanation: A lactating mare can drink 50â80 liters per day, especially in hot climates.

quiz.q: What is the most common cause of endometritis in mares?
options: B) Bacterial infection from poor breeding hygiene
quiz.explanation: Bacteria like Streptococcus zooepidemicus often enter the uterus during breeding if hygiene is poor.

quiz.q: What treatment is used for uterine infection in a problem mare?
options: A) Uterine lavage with saline and antibiotics
quiz.explanation: Lavage with saline removes debris, and antibiotics kill bacteria; this is the standard treatment.

quiz.q: What is a sign of pneumovagina?
options: B) Air sucked into the vagina, often with a noise
quiz.explanation: Pneumovagina occurs when air is drawn into the vagina due to poor vulvar conformation.

quiz.q: How much protein should a pregnant mare receive in late gestation?
quiz.explanation: Late gestation requires 12â14% protein to support rapid fetal growth.

quiz.q: Which mineral is often deficient in African soils and important for reproduction?
quiz.explanation: Selenium deficiency is common in many African regions and can cause infertility and weak foals.

quiz.q: How often should a mare be dewormed during the breeding season?
options: D) Only when she shows signs of worms
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 8â12 weeks controls internal parasites that can affect health and fertility.

quiz.q: What is the best way to increase energy for a thin mare?
options: B) Add grains like oats or maize
quiz.explanation: Grains provide concentrated energy to help a thin mare gain weight and start cycling.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of a mare with a persistent corpus luteum?
quiz.explanation: A persistent corpus luteum produces progesterone, suppressing estrus for an abnormally long time.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of hCG to induce ovulation?
quiz.explanation: 1500â2500 IU of hCG is standard for inducing ovulation in mares.

quiz.q: Why is it important to scan a mare at 28â30 days of pregnancy?
options: B) To confirm a heartbeat and check for twins
quiz.explanation: At 28â30 days, a heartbeat is visible, and twins can be detected and managed to avoid abortion.

quiz.q: What is a 'problem mare'?
options: B) A mare that fails to conceive after three breeding cycles
C) A mare that is too old
D) A mare that refuses to eat
quiz.explanation: A problem mare is defined as one that does not become pregnant after multiple breeding attempts.

quiz.q: Which of these is a practical way to synchronize mares in Africa?
options: B) Using a teaser stallion only
quiz.explanation: Prostaglandin is widely used and effective for synchronizing mares when a corpus luteum is present.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a uterine biopsy in a breeding soundness exam?
options: B) To assess fibrosis and inflammation
quiz.explanation: A biopsy reveals the degree of fibrosis and inflammation, which helps predict fertility.

quiz.q: How can you prevent pneumovagina in a mare with poor conformation?
quiz.explanation: Caslick's suture closes the upper vulva, preventing air and feces from entering the vagina.

quiz.q: What is the recommended energy increase for a mare in late gestation?
quiz.explanation: Energy needs increase by 10â20% in late gestation to support fetal growth.
